```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", eval = FALSE)
```

In about five minutes, you can find a public parks dataset, load a small
preview into R, and make a chart. You only need basic R: no mapping software
or knowledge of the publisher's data service is required. Run the commands
in order. Searching the package's catalog works offline; retrieving records
needs an internet connection. The publisher can change its data, so your
results may differ from another person's or from a later run.

## 1. Install the package

Install the package from CRAN once:

```{r install}
install.packages("tampaBayOpenData")
```

Load it each time you start a new R session:

```{r load-package, eval=TRUE}
library(tampaBayOpenData)
```

## 2. Find a dataset

Search for parks in the package's checked catalog:

```{r find-parks, eval=TRUE}
matches <- tbod_search_datasets("parks", source = "checked")
matches[, c("id", "title")]
```

A **dataset** is a collection of related records published by an organization.
Each row in these search results points to one dataset, with a title and an
`id` that you can use to retrieve it. `source = "checked"` searches the
package's built-in list of datasets whose structures have been inspected.
This search does not download park records. Find the `hillsborough-parks` row;
that is the ID we will use for the rest of this tutorial. The list can grow
when the package is updated.

## 3. Download some records

Ask Hillsborough County's public service for a small preview:

```{r retrieve-parks}
parks <- tbod_get_dataset("hillsborough-parks", limit = 100)
```

`tbod_get_dataset()` retrieves public records and puts them in `parks`, a
table you can explore in R. No account or password is needed. `limit = 100`
requests up to 100 records; if more match, these are only some of them. They
are the first records returned by the service, not a random sample. In this
source, each row describes a mapped property area managed by the county;
several rows can describe the same park. Run this line in your R session to
see the publisher's current records.

## 4. Explore what you found

Start with three familiar ways to inspect a table:

```{r inspect-parks}
head(parks)
nrow(parks)
names(parks)
```

`head()` shows the first few rows, `nrow()` tells you how many rows arrived,
and `names()` lists the columns. The publisher supplies these columns. One
of them, `USES`, labels how each property is used. Which labels appear most
often in the records you received?

```{r count-uses}
park_uses <- table(parks$USES, useNA = "ifany")
park_uses <- sort(park_uses, decreasing = TRUE)
park_uses
```

`table()` counts records for each use label, including a missing-value group
if one appears. `sort()` puts the largest counts first. These counts describe
only the returned preview; they do not tell you how many parks of each type
exist across the county.

## 5. Make your first chart

Show the five most common use labels in that same preview:

```{r chart-uses}
top_uses <- head(park_uses, 5)
barplot(top_uses, horiz = TRUE, las = 1, cex.names = 0.7,
        col = "steelblue", xlab = "Property records",
        main = "Most common uses in this preview")
```

Each bar counts property records with one of the publisher's use labels.
The chart is a quick look at the rows you loaded, not an estimate for all
county parks. The first 100 records may change, and mapped property outlines
do not establish legal boundaries, public access, or opening hours. If the
service is temporarily unavailable, try the retrieval again later; the
[retrieval guide's troubleshooting section](retrieval.html#troubleshooting-common-errors)
has more help.

## What to try next

You found a dataset, retrieved a small table, inspected its columns, counted
use labels, and made a chart. To explore another topic, change the search
word, choose an `id` from the results, and inspect `names()` before counting
a column. The [discovery guide](discovery.html) helps you find more datasets;
the [retrieval guide](retrieval.html) covers filters and larger downloads.
When you are ready for maps, try the [spatial example](mapping-capital-improvements.html).
For longer real-world walkthroughs, see [housing](housing-development.html),
[water quality](water-quality.html), and
[infrastructure](infrastructure-projects.html).
